d: Full mock interview: design a notification system
goal: Your win today: given 'design a notification system', you can scope it in 5 minutes, sketch the queue-based design, defend reliability/dedupe/retries and the guardrails under 'what if X fails?', and wrap up with the book's five points plus what you'd do next.
bookSections: Whole chapter via the 4-step framework: Step 1 scope Q&A, Step 2 high-level design (improved), Step 3 deep dive (reliability, additional components, updated design), Step 4 wrap-up

stages.title: Scope it
stages.teaches: The book's clarifying Q&A: types → push, SMS and email; real-time → soft real-time (ASAP, slight delay OK under heavy load); devices → iOS, Android, laptop/desktop; triggers → client applications, or scheduled on the server side; opt-out → yes, opted-out users receive nothing; volume → 10M mobile push, 1M SMS, 5M email per day. Good extra questions to earn signal: priority/transactional vs marketing, ordering needs, international markets.
stages.interaction: Same mechanic as 0008: interviewer chat bubble says 'Design a notification system.' A game clock (45 min) and a question deck of ~10 cards. Good cards (each reveals the book's answer onto a Requirements board and costs 1 game-minute): notification types, real-time or not, supported devices, what triggers them, can users opt out, daily volume, (bonus) are some messages critical like login codes, (bonus) which countries. Time-wasters (cost 3 minutes and signal): 'Which programming language?', 'What colour is the badge?', 'Should we use Kafka or RabbitMQ?' (premature). Then a lock-in quiz: 'Which is the book's volume?' Correct: '10M push, 1M SMS, 5M email per day'. Distractors: swap the numbers (e.g. '10M email, 5M SMS, 1M push'), '16M per hour', '1B per day'.
stages.check: Requirements board must show all 6 book answers; lock-in quiz answered.

stages.title: Sketch it
stages.sub: Step 2 · high-level design and buy-in (10–15 min)
stages.teaches: Start with the contact-info flow and the four channels (APNs, FCM, SMS provider, email provider), state the naive one-server design's 3 problems in one breath, then draw the improved design: services → notification servers (autoscaled) with cache + DB → per-channel queues → workers → third parties → devices; narrate the 6-step flow. Get interviewer buy-in before diving deeper.
stages.interaction: Tap-to-draw like 0008: component palette (Services 1..N, Load balancer, Notification servers, Cache, DB, iOS PN queue, Android PN queue, SMS queue, Email queue, Workers, APNs, FCM, SMS provider, Email provider, plus decoys: 'One big queue', 'Workers call DB for every field', 'Services call APNs directly'). Learner taps components in drawing order; a component whose dependency isn't drawn yet costs 1 minute; a decoy costs a heart with an explanation (e.g. services calling APNs directly = every team re-implements auth, settings, retry). Interviewer then asks 'Why not one queue?' quiz → 'Isolation: an SMS outage must not block push and email'.
stages.check: Diagram complete; 'why per-channel queues' quiz answered.

stages.title: The technique map
stages.sub: Step 3 · every requirement needs a mechanism
stages.teaches: Requirement → mechanism map: never lose a notification → notification log + retry (ack after send); no duplicates (mostly) → dedupe by event ID; one provider outage isolated → per-channel queues; bursts → queue buffering + autoscaling servers; failures persist → alert developers; workers falling behind → monitor queued notifications, add workers; spam/unauthorised senders → auth with appKey/appSecret; user overwhelm → rate limiting + opt-in settings; consistent messages → templates; understanding engagement → events tracking + analytics service.
stages.interaction: Match board: 10 requirement cards on the left, 10 mechanism cards on the right (shuffled). Learner taps a requirement then a mechanism to draw a line; correct pairs lock, wrong ones cost a minute. When complete, the mechanisms light up on the Step 2 diagram where they live (log next to workers, auth/rate-limit on servers, etc.) — producing the book's updated design.

stages.title: Boss: the curveball barrage
stages.teaches: Failure follow-ups and the senior answers: APNs outage → iOS queue grows, retries with backoff, other channels unaffected, alert if prolonged; worker crash after send → duplicate possible, dedupe reduces it; notification server dies → stateless, LB routes around it; queue broker dies → queues must be replicated (book is silent); DB/cache outage → cache hit keeps sends going, DB replicas, servers may shed or delay low-priority work; stale tokens → delete on 410/UNREGISTERED; 10× campaign spike → queue absorbs, autoscale workers, rate-limit marketing; login-code SMS stuck behind a campaign → separate high-priority queue; one SMS provider down for hours → failover to a second provider (extensibility).
stages.interaction: Custom curveball rounds (like 0008, not the fixed-choice Q.boss): 7 interviewer questions, each with its own 3 answer options (one senior, one junior-but-plausible, one wrong). E.g. 'APNs is down for 20 minutes. What happens?' → senior: 'iOS queue backs up and retries with backoff; Android, SMS and email keep flowing because queues are per channel; we alert if it persists' / junior: 'Workers retry immediately in a tight loop until it's back' / wrong: 'We drop iOS notifications during the outage'. Others: worker crash after send; queue broker loses a node; 10× Black Friday spike; login code waiting behind a 5M-email campaign; SMS provider down for hours; thousands of 410 Unregistered responses. Correct = +XP; junior = no hearts lost but no XP plus the senior answer shown; wrong = heart lost.

stages.title: Wrap it up
stages.teaches: Book's wrap-up: the system is scalable, supports push, SMS and email, and uses message queues to decouple components. Highlights: reliability (robust retry mechanism to minimise failure rate), security (appKey/appSecret so only verified clients send), tracking and monitoring (capture stats at every stage), respecting user settings (check opt-in before sending), rate limiting (frequency cap users appreciate). Good 'next steps' beyond the book: priority queues for transactional messages, multi-provider failover, dead-letter queues, token hygiene, localisation of templates, queue replication.
stages.interaction: Pick-your-closer: a grid of 10 talking-point cards; learner has room for 5 'minutes' of wrap-up and picks cards (each costs 1). Scored: the book's 5 points score full signal; 'next steps' cards score bonus signal only after at least 3 book points are chosen; filler cards ('I'd use microservices everywhere', 'Rewrite it in Rust') cost signal. Then a quiz: 'Which of these is NOT in the book's wrap-up list?' Correct: 'Exactly-once delivery guarantee'. Distractors: 'Respect user settings', 'Rate limiting', 'Security with appKey/appSecret'.

stages.title: Say it like a senior
stages.interaction: Q.drill, then a scorecard summarising game-minutes used, signal earned, hearts left per step (stored under a separate key, e.g. 'sdq:v1:<this quest id>-interview', as 0008 does). Prompt: 'Give me the whole design in about a minute.' Model: 'Scope: push, SMS and email; soft real-time; iOS, Android and desktop; triggered by services or schedules; users can opt out; about 10 million pushes, 1 million SMS and 5 million emails a day. We collect device tokens, phones and emails at install and signup. Services call an authenticated, rate-limited API on stateless notification servers, which check the user's opt-in settings, fill a template, look up tokens from cache and DB, and enqueue to one queue per channel. Workers pull, log each notification, and call APNs, FCM, the SMS provider or the email provider. Failed sends are retried with backoff, and persistent failures alert us; nothing is lost, though it may be late. Exactly-once is impossible, so we dedupe by event ID. We monitor queue depth to add workers, and track sent, delivered, clicked and unsubscribed in analytics.' Checks: 'I scoped with the book's numbers and requirements', 'I drew servers → per-channel queues → workers → providers', 'I covered reliability (log, retry, dedupe) and the guardrails (auth, settings, rate limit, templates, tracking)'.

caveats: The book never computes QPS for this chapter; quoting ~185/s average and stressing burstiness is our addition and a good way to earn signal.
The book splits queues by channel only; adding priority (transactional vs marketing) and replicating the queues are senior-level extensions, not book content.
Exactly-once delivery is impossible end to end; say 'at-least-once with dedupe' rather than promising exactly-once.
The 45-minute game clock and step timings follow the book's framework chapter; real interview loops vary.
